subject: 2023-count
title: Number of Ways to Traverse a Grid

plan.A: Research an exact sparse-obstacle candidate for low M: deduplicate blocked coordinates, sort them in a valid dependency order, and use binomial path counts with inclusion-exclusion to compute paths avoiding earlier obstacles, then evaluate the destination. Precompute factorials and inverse factorials modulo 1000000007 (the largest needed factorial index is below the modulus). Handle blocked start or destination and N=1 explicitly. The pairwise work can be O(M^2), so do not assume the stated M bound makes M small: include a cost-based switch or exact fallback for larger M. Check duplicate obstacles and coordinate ordering against the baseline semantics.
plan.B: Optimize the dense row-DP as an independently correct, linear-memory candidate. Replace the N-by-N blocked grid with O(N+M) storage, such as per-row sorted blocked columns; use two O(N) DP rows and swap them instead of copying a row each iteration. Preserve the row recurrence, modular arithmetic, and output exactly. Focus on memory and practical dense-case performance; the O(N^2) traversal remains. Measure arithmetic or representation changes rather than assuming they help, and retain a correct path for all valid inputs.
plan.C: Investigate an exact four-core parallel implementation of the dense DP. Within each row, blocked cells reset the recurrence; each open run is an inclusive prefix sum of the previous row's values. Explore a parallel segmented scan with correct handling of runs crossing chunk boundaries, while keeping row dependencies sequential. Benchmark parallel overhead, especially on small cases, and use no more than the available four CPU cores. Do not rely on GPU or on changing the compiler or evaluation setup.
plan.G: Evaluate A, B, and C candidates standalone for correctness and runtime under the unchanged evaluation setup before integrating anything. Consider a measured hybrid such as sparse combinatorial handling for low M and a linear-memory DP fallback, but derive dispatch from general cost/performance evidence, not particular test inputs. Re-test the integrated program: gains may not add, and a combination can be slower than its components. Keep the fastest correct option, preserve behavior for every valid input, and verify blocked endpoints, duplicates, modular results, and output formatting.
plan.analysis: The supplied source is the grid-path problem (Problem D). Its baseline is correct on 4 cases and measured at a mean of 0.079210793 seconds (individual times about 0.07918–0.07923 seconds), with score 0.5; no alternative measurements are available, so no speedup is established. The source allocates an N-by-N blocked grid and performs O(N^2) DP work, while the statement permits N below 200000 and only gives an upper bound on M that does not guarantee M is small enough for an O(M^2) method. The main research directions are therefore exact sparse handling with a safe fallback, reducing dense-path memory, and testing whether intra-row parallelism pays on the ARM64 four-core, no-GPU target.

plan.A: Research the sparse-obstacle combinatorial method: count monotone paths using binomial coefficients and inclusion-exclusion over sorted, deduplicated blocked cells. Handle blocked endpoints, N=1, and modular arithmetic for all valid inputs. Tune a generic work-based crossover against the dense DP. In this run, the measured A variants took 56.4 ms and 62.0 ms; the stricter pair-work threshold was faster, so do not broaden the sparse branch without evidence.
plan.B: Refine the segmented rolling-row DP with AArch64 NEON scans, using the 20.6 ms candidate as the current performance lead. Focus on safe scan/carry propagation within open segments, scalar tails and fallback, and correctness at obstacle boundaries. Preserve a portable scalar path and compare whole-program measurements; do not assume vector gains transfer to other architectures or combine additively with other candidates.
plan.C: Explore four-core row-chunk parallel scans while preserving the sequential row dependency, O(N+M) obstacle storage, and exact modular segmented-prefix behavior. Reduce per-row synchronization and carry overhead, and use a generic size/work threshold only if measurements support it. The two measured OpenMP candidates took 30.1 ms and 31.0 ms, slower than B's 20.6 ms, so treat parallelization as an experiment rather than an assumed win.
plan.G: Use B's 20.6 ms candidate as the initial integration reference, but compare complete integrated programs rather than adding standalone speedups. Evaluate A's sparse branch only as a measured alternative to the dense scan, and retain C only if it improves end-to-end results. Gate integration on correctness for all valid inputs, including blocked endpoints and duplicate obstacles; preserve a portable fallback and remeasure after each integration.
plan.analysis: Problem D's baseline stores an N×N blocked grid and performs serial O(N²) DP; the official large-N sparsity condition makes O(N+M) obstacle storage important, though a dense cell scan still costs O(N²). The correct baseline measured 79.2 ms on this ARM64, four-core target. Reported candidate means were B 20.6 ms, C 30.1/31.0 ms, and A 56.4/62.0 ms. These measurements favor B as the present reference, not as proof that a combined or different-workload program will be faster. Keep the recurrence equivalent modulo 1,000,000,007 and validate the full integrated program.
